args.text:
Committee Policy Actions
No word of a lie, here's how it went down at the Yanks' version of the RBA board. To back the Committee's dual-mandate goals, every last member agreed to whack the target range for the federal funds rate up 1/4 percentage point, to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, and they stuck by the FOMC's policy of keeping ample reserves in the banking system, same as ever. Members noted the unemployment rate had hardly budged, and the economy was still growing at a solid clip, with domestic spending holding up like a good bloke in a stoush, while inflation was still sitting up there, a fair way above the Committee's 2 percent goal. So the Committee made it dead plain it's not mucking about on its dual-mandate goals, putting it right there in the postmeeting statement that it "will deliver price stability." Not "hope to", mind. And members reckoned the policy action they'd just taken would get inflation back to the Committee's 2 percent goal sooner.

Once they'd talked it all out, the Committee voted to tell the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, until it hears otherwise, to carry out transactions in the System Open Market Account in line with the following domestic policy directive, out at 2:00 p.m. on the dot. Here it is, word for word:

"Effective September 17, 2026, the Federal Open Market Committee directs the Desk to:

Undertake open market operations as necessary to maintain the federal funds rate in a target range of 3-3/4 to 4 percent.

Conduct standing overnight repurchase agreement operations at a rate of 4.0 percent.

Conduct standing overnight reverse repurchase agreement operations at an offering rate of 3.75 percent and with a per-counterparty limit of $160 billion per day.

When appropriate, increase the System Open Market Account holdings of securities through purchases of Treasury bills and, if needed, other Treasury securities with remaining maturities of 3 years or less to maintain an ample level of reserves.

Roll over at auction all principal payments from the Federal Reserve's holdings of Treasury securities. Reinvest all principal payments from the Federal Reserve's holdings of agency securities into Treasury bills."

That same vote gave the nod to the statement below as well, also out at 2:00 p.m. Word for word again:

"The Federal Open Market Committee approved the following statement for release by a 12–0 vote:

The Committee decided to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 1/4 percentage point to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate. The Committee is continuing its policy of maintaining ample reserves in the banking system.

Economic activity is expanding at a solid pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.

Inflation remains elevated. Today's policy action will support a timelier return to the Committee's 2 percent goal. The Committee will deliver price stability."

Who put their hand up for it: Kevin Warsh, John C. Williams, Michael S. Barr, Michelle W. Bowman, Lisa D. Cook, Beth M. Hammack, Philip N. Jefferson, Neel Kashkari, Lorie K. Logan, Anna Paulson, Jerome H. Powell, and Christopher J. Waller. The whole box and dice.

Voting against this action: None. Not a peep.

And to go with the Committee lifting the target range for the federal funds rate to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System voted unanimously to bump the interest rate paid on reserve balances up to 3.90 percent, effective September 17, 2026. Then the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, unanimous again, gave a 1/4 percentage point increase in the primary credit rate the nod as well, taking it to 4.0 percent, effective September 17, 2026.2

They've pencilled in the Committee's next get-together for Tuesday–Wednesday, October 27–28, 2026. And they called it a day at 10:15 a.m. on September 16, 2026, well before smoko.

Notation Vote
One more bit of housekeeping: by notation vote completed on August 18, 2026, the Committee unanimously signed off on the minutes of the Committee meeting held on July 28–29, 2026.
